prize_parts.citation: for showing how credit limits tied to collateral values and asset prices feed back on each other, so that shocks are amplified and propagated into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: B011, Kiyotaki and Moore only. The scientific case is the 1997 mechanism. Borrowing limits depend on collateral values, collateral values depend on borrowing, and so small temporary shocks become large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism is general and tractable, and it has been reused for almost three decades as a building block of macro-finance and of the financial-friction models used in policy work. The credit follows from one two-author paper, so no line has to be drawn through a diffuse literature. In round 2 I re-tested the case against the strongest rival, B005, and against the chair's questions. What I changed is narrower than the preference. First, the citation now says what is and is not honoured: the collateral-price feedback is, while the net-worth and external-finance-premium accelerator and the bank-run and bank-crisis literature are not. Second, I have dropped B019 as a listed alternative. Eight credited names against a three-person cap is an attribution problem I cannot resolve, and nothing in round 1 resolved it. I now list B014 as the second alternative. I ranked B014 fourth at the opening, and it has the longest replication record among the labour candidates. Six round-1 preferences for B011 equal the six-vote threshold, but that count includes my own position and that of a frequent co-author, so I do not treat it as evidence of merit. My judgment rests on attribution, maturity and mechanism clarity. I would support B005 in a single-part prize if colleagues conclude that the 2022 overlap is decisive against B011.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one all six B011 supporters record. The 2022 prize recognised research on banks and financial crises, and a committee could reasonably judge that financial frictions in macro are already honoured. I think the mechanisms differ, but that judgment is contestable. The second objection is identification. The collateral channel is established mainly as a mechanism and modelling building block, and much less as a measured magnitude. Evidence comes from crisis episodes, calibrated models and adjacent household and firm studies, and the direct micro evidence is thinner than the firm-level evidence behind B005. Third, a two-name award leaves out the quantitative accelerator and intermediation work of Gertler and Gilchrist, which carried the ideas into policy models. That is a real cost in completeness, and I accept it for the sake of a clean and defensible citation. Finally, this is an assessment from general knowledge. I have not independently verified any source, and my field is adjacent, so I may be a generous reader of macro-finance theory.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B005 because firm-level data across many countries support the selection and reallocation margins directly. He argues that the collateral channel is harder to identify and that the 2022 overlap blurs the marginal case for B011. He would anchor the B005 citation on the theoretical integration of firm heterogeneity into trade.
responses.response: The directness of the evidence is B005's real advantage over B011, and I do not dismiss it. I weigh it differently, though. A prize can honour a mechanism whose reuse as a building block is the main evidence of its importance, provided the citation does not claim a measured effect size. That is why my wording credits the feedback mechanism and says nothing about the size of the amplification. On your question about a two-name B011 with a clearly separated citation, my answer is that this wording was written to do that. On attribution I think B005 is harder to defend, because Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum sit outside the credited names and Helpman's marginal credit has to be stated apart from Krugman's 2008 recognition and apart from B020. Your wording solves part of that. It does not solve the question of who is being honoured. If the committee settled that point convincingly, I would support Helpman and Melitz.

responses.point: Boppart now puts B005 first, with B011 as his first alternative. He says the choice is closer than his opening ranks suggest. He would word the B005 citation around firm heterogeneity and selection and not around the empirical discovery of exporter premia, and he would not add a third name to B011.
responses.response: We agree on the two-name B011 and on keeping Redding out of B005, and I am glad the choice looks close to you as well. The wording you propose for B005 is the one I could support. It credits Melitz's model and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension and makes no claim on Bernard and Jensen's empirical facts or on Eaton-Kortum. We still differ on how to rank attribution against directness of evidence. I rank clean attribution higher for a prize that must name specific people for a specific discovery. I do not see this as a gap in scientific quality, and I would not block B005 if the committee preferred it. Because we co-author, I note that my reading of your argument is independent of that tie and that I have tried to apply common criteria.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B005 because its central mechanism has been tested against micro data. She says the 2022 overlap weighs more heavily with her than the other files allow, and she qualifies the claim that the 2007-09 crisis confirmed the collateral mechanism.
responses.response: I accept the qualification. The crisis does not pin down the quantitative size of the amplification, and I would not defend the mechanism on that ground. The case rests on conceptual clarity, longevity and repeated use. On the 2022 overlap, I read that prize as being about banks and their role in crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns real-economy amplification through collateral values and asset prices. The mechanisms are related but distinct, and I think the citation can say so. I cannot show that you would find this convincing, and it remains the main thing the committee has to decide. I agree with your decision to set B019 aside. I did the same, and I replaced it with B014 as an alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B011 first with Kiyotaki and Moore. She treats the 2022 overlap as a framing issue for the citation, accepts that the strongest evidence is reuse as a building block, and lists B014 as her first alternative while noting overlap with the 2023 and 2024 prizes and a contested China-shock literature.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap can be handled in the citation, and the revised wording tries to do that. Your caution on B014 is also one I share. I have moved B014 into my alternatives because it is a well-scrutinised labour candidate, but its third name is open (Katz or Dorn, as the chair notes), I still think the credit for the task framework sits partly with Acemoglu and Restrepo, and the persistence of the China-shock effects is debated. My own round-1 proposal of Autor and Hanson reflects that. I would support a B014 configuration only if those points are addressed in the wording, and I would not give it priority over B011 or B005.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B012 but now treats B005 and B011 as having cleaner attribution. He says B011's 2022 overlap concern is answerable. His own caveats on B012 are cross-country identification, dispersion across many contributors, and field adjacency.
responses.response: Your openness to B011 and B005 helps, because the single-part comparison is the real decision. I considered B012 and left it out of my alternatives. The three-name grouping is natural, but I weigh identification, dispersion and the 2024 institutions prize more heavily than you do, and I think the case should rest on later state-capacity work and on the theory, as you say. Your question to me is where I would go if B011 did not carry. B005. I also note your point that recent recognition of a theme does not by itself show that a different mechanism has been honoured. I apply that to B011 and the 2022 prize as well.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee should give the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises when judging collateral-based amplification. My view is that the mechanisms differ, but this is a judgment and not a finding.

Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist undercredits the quantitative accelerator and intermediation strand that brought financial frictions into policy models. Several colleagues, including Hjalmarsson and Stromberg, say they would not object if the committee decided otherwise.
How much indirect empirical identification should count against a foundational theory contribution, compared with B005's more direct firm-level testing.

For B005, whether wording alone can handle the missing names (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum), Helpman's marginal credit relative to Krugman 2008 and B020, and the possible Melitz-centred single-name option.
Whether a coherent two-part pairing exists under the three-person cap. I have not found one that does not weaken the clean attribution of B011, so I propose a single part.
All assessments rely on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 text. I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist is apparent from the supplied profile, and none to Helpman, Melitz or Redding either. I disclose long-standing co-authorship with committee colleagues John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart, and I am the committee's secretary. Hassler is a B011 supporter and Boppart now prefers B005, and I have tried to weigh each argument on its substance. My own research (heterogeneous-agent macro, growth, climate-economy modelling) is adjacent to macro-finance, so I may be a generous reader of B011. My earlier co-authors listed in the profile (for example Smith, Ríos-Rull, Violante, Greenwood, Tsyvinski) are not credited on any shortlisted entry that I propose. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
